The paper "From Local to Global: A GraphRAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization" addresses the challenge of answering global questions over large text corpora, which retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems typically fail to address effectively. Traditional vector RAG methods excel at retrieving localized information but fall short when queries require synthesizing global insights, such as identifying key themes or trends across an entire dataset. Query-focused summarization (QFS) methods also struggle to scale with the large volumes of text typically indexed by RAG systems. The paper introduces GraphRAG, a graph-based RAG method that combines knowledge graph construction with hierarchical summarization to enable global sensemaking.

GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph from source documents, partitions it into thematic communities using hierarchical Leiden community detection, and generates summaries for each community. When a query is posed, each community summary generates a partial answer, which are then combined into a global answer through a map-reduce process. The method is evaluated using a novel LLM-as-a-judge technique and compared to vector RAG and a global text summarization method (TS) on two real-world datasets totaling approximately 1.7 million tokens.

Results show that GraphRAG significantly outperforms vector RAG in terms of answer comprehensiveness and diversity, with win rates of 67.6% (p. 8) for comprehensiveness and 65.3% (p. 8) for diversity across both datasets. For the Podcast dataset, global methods (C0–C3) had win rates of 72–83% in comprehensiveness and 75–82% in diversity, while for the News dataset, the win rates were 72–80% and 62–71%, respectively. Root-level GraphRAG summaries required over 97% fewer tokens than source text summarization (p. 9). However, vector RAG produced the most direct responses. Community summaries showed small but consistent improvements in comprehensiveness and diversity over source texts, except for root-level summaries. LLM-based win rates aligned with claim-based metrics in 78% of comprehensiveness comparisons and 69–70% for diversity, indicating moderately strong alignment (p. 11).
